title: Life Insurance
description: Term, whole life, and the years of income a household would lose.
wolfLine: Insure the paycheck. Do not insure a slogan.

term-life.definition: Life insurance that pays if you die during a set period, such as 20 years. It is insurance, not an investment account.
term-life.example: A 20-year term policy for $500,000 might cost $25 a month. If you outlive the term, it does not pay.

whole-life.definition: Life insurance meant to last your whole life, with a savings piece inside. The premium is much higher than term for the same death benefit.
whole-life.example: The same $500,000 might cost $220 a month as whole life. Most of the extra premium is the savings piece and the lifetime promise.

beneficiary.definition: The person, or people, who receive the life insurance money if you die.
beneficiary.example: You name your sister. If you die while the policy is in force, she receives the death benefit, not your email provider.

lessons.title: Who Needs Life Insurance
lessons.summary: Insure the paycheck someone else depends on.

steps.context: Life insurance pays a death benefit to the people who lose your income. [[Term life insurance|term-life]] is the usual way to buy a large benefit for a set number of years.
steps.prompt: Who has the clearest reason to buy life insurance?
choices: A parent whose income pays the rent
A single adult no one relies on for money
A person who wants a fancy savings slogan
steps.explain: The question is who would be short of money if you died.

steps.prompt: Life insurance is a good fit when no person and no debt depends on your income.
steps.explain: If nobody is harmed financially by your death, the premium has little to protect.

steps.prompt: A stay-at-home parent provides childcare that would cost money to replace. Do they have a reason to be insured?
choices: Yes. Replacing that care costs real money
No. Only paychecks count
No. Children cannot be beneficiaries
steps.explain: The loss is the cost of replacing the care, not only a W-2.

steps.prompt: What is the death benefit?
choices: The amount paid if you die while the policy is in force
The monthly premium
A bonus for staying healthy
steps.explain: That check is the point of the policy.

steps.prompt: Buy life insurance to protect people who ___ your income or your care.
choices: depend on
compete with
insure
steps.explain: No dependent, no job for this policy.

lessons.title: Term or Whole Life
lessons.summary: Same death benefit. A very different price.

steps.context: [[Term life insurance|term-life]] covers a period. [[Whole life insurance|whole-life]] is priced to last, and to carry savings.
steps.prompt: What is the term quote per year?
What is the whole life quote per year?
How much more is whole life per year, for the same $500,000?
You want a large benefit while your kids are growing up, and you will invest the rest yourself. Which quote fits?
choices: The term quote
The whole life quote
Neither. The benefits differ
why: Whole life costs $2,340 more for the same benefit.
steps.explain: Term buys the $500,000 for $300 a year. The extra $2,340 is not more death benefit.

steps.prompt: Whole life is more expensive because it pays a larger death benefit in this pair of quotes.
steps.explain: Both say $500,000. The price difference is the lifetime design and the savings piece.

lessons.title: How Much
lessons.summary: A plain estimate: years of income the household would lose.

steps.title: A rough replacement
steps.body:
A common starting point is several years of the income your household would lose. Ten years is a simple sketch, not a personal plan.

If you earn **$50,000** a year, ten years is **$500,000**. Debts, a partner’s income, and savings move that number.

steps.prompt: Ten years of a $50,000 income. What is that sketch?
You earn $40,000. Ten years. What is the sketch?
The sketch is $400,000 and you already have $50,000 in life insurance through work. How much is the gap?
The ten-year sketch is a personal order you must follow.
steps.explain: It is a starting sketch. A partner’s paycheck or a paid-off home can shrink it.

lessons.title: The Policy Page
lessons.summary: Benefit, price, term, and the name of the person who is paid.

steps.context: The page should name the [[beneficiary]]: the person who receives the money.
steps.prompt: What death benefit does this policy page list?
steps.explain: That line is $500,000.

steps.prompt: What yearly premium does this policy page list?
steps.explain: That line is $300.

steps.prompt: Who receives the money if you die while this policy is in force?
choices: The beneficiary named on the policy
Whoever finds the paper
The insurer’s shareholders
steps.explain: The name on the policy is the instruction.

steps.prompt: A 20-year term pays the death benefit if you die in year 25.
steps.explain: The term ended. Outliving it means no payout, which is what you hope for.

steps.prompt: Why write the beneficiary down instead of assuming the family will sort it out?
choices: The policy pays the name it has, not the argument that follows
Insurers ignore the form
A will always overrides every beneficiary
steps.explain: The form is the instruction the insurer follows.

lessons.title: Beneficiaries
lessons.summary: The form is the will for this one check.

steps.context: Keep the [[beneficiary]] current. A divorce, a baby, or a death can make the old name wrong.
steps.prompt: What is a beneficiary?
choices: The person you name to receive the death benefit
The agent who sold the policy
The hospital
steps.explain: No name, and the money waits on a process your family did not need.

steps.prompt: Naming your beneficiary once, at age 22, is enough for life.
steps.explain: Life changes. The form does not update itself.

steps.prompt: You have a baby and the beneficiary is still a parent who has died. What do you do?
choices: Update the form
Wait for the insurer to notice
Cancel the policy
steps.explain: A dead beneficiary sends the money into a slower process.

steps.prompt: You want your partner and your sibling to split the benefit. What does the form need?
choices: Both names, and the share each one gets
Only a nickname
The word family
steps.explain: Shares should add to the whole. Write the percents.

steps.prompt: You leave 60% to your partner and 40% to your sibling. What do the shares add up to?

lessons.title: Coverage Through Work
lessons.summary: It is a start. It leaves when the job does.

steps.context: Work coverage is often one or two times your salary. [[COBRA|cobra]] is about health insurance after a job ends, not a promise that the life policy stays.
steps.prompt: What is the usual limit of life insurance you get at work?
choices: It often ends when the job ends, and the benefit can be small
It follows you for life at the same price
It replaces a term policy dollar for dollar, always
steps.explain: A job change can take the coverage with it.

steps.prompt: Your salary is $50,000. Work life insurance is one times salary. What is the benefit?
Your ten-year sketch is $500,000. How much of that sketch is missing?
Quitting the job keeps that work policy in force at no cost.
steps.explain: The policy belonged to the job. Ask what, if anything, you can take with you, and at what price.

steps.prompt: Why not rely on the work policy alone while you have young kids?
choices: The benefit is often only a year or two of pay, and it can end with the job
Work policies are illegal
Kids cannot be protected by any policy
steps.explain: One year of pay is a thin bridge.

lessons.title: Why Most People Choose Term
lessons.summary: Buy the protection. Invest the difference on purpose.

steps.prompt: Why do many people choose term instead of whole life?
choices: Term buys a large benefit for a small premium during the years people depend on you
Term pays a larger death benefit for the same premium in the quotes we used
Whole life is illegal
steps.explain: The expensive years are the years with kids or a big debt. Term covers those years.

steps.prompt: Term is $300 a year. Whole life is $2,640. How much is left each year if you buy term instead?
That $2,340 is automatically a better investment if you spend it.
steps.explain: The difference only helps if you actually save or invest it. Spending it buys neither insurance nor savings.

steps.prompt: You have no dependents and no co-signed debt. What is a reasonable conclusion?
choices: You may not need life insurance right now
You must buy whole life
You must buy the largest term sold
steps.explain: The product protects a person. No person, no purchase required.

steps.prompt: Term covers a ___ of years, not your whole life by default.
choices: set number
random
secret
steps.explain: When the term ends, so does the coverage.

lessons.title: Aisha and Her New Baby
lessons.summary: One year of pay is not ten.

story.title: A paycheck and a new baby
story.body:
Aisha’s baby is three months old. She earns **$4,000** a month, **$48,000** a year. Her partner works too, but the rent still needs her paycheck. Work gives her life insurance equal to one year of pay, **$48,000**.

A ten-year sketch of her income is **$480,000**. A 20-year term quote for that amount is **$28** a month.

steps.prompt: What is ten years of Aisha’s $48,000 income?
How much of that sketch does the work policy already cover?
steps.explain: One year of pay is $48,000.

steps.prompt: How big is the gap?
The term quote is $28 a month. What is that per year?
What is the sensible shape of her next step?
choices: Price a term policy for the gap, and name the baby’s other parent as beneficiary
Buy whole life because a baby means the expensive product
Drop the work policy and stay uninsured
steps.explain: The gap is the uncovered years. Term is built for a gap with an end date.

lessons.title: Sharpen Up
lessons.summary: Smart repetition on what you’re closest to forgetting.

lessons.title: Den Trial: Life Insurance
lessons.summary: 8 questions. Three strikes and you’re out.

steps.prompt: Life insurance is most useful when:
choices: Someone depends on your income
You want a logo on a folder
You have no dependents and no shared debts
steps.explain: The benefit replaces what those people would lose.

steps.prompt: Term premium $40 a month. What is the yearly premium?
A work life policy of one times salary usually equals a ten-year income sketch.
steps.explain: One times salary is one year, not ten.

steps.prompt: Who should you name on the policy?
choices: The beneficiary who should receive the money
Whoever sold it
No one. The form is optional
steps.explain: The name is the instruction.
